description: Flat 8 m square of red clay brick paving laid in a herringbone pattern -- one quad, one seamless PBR texture set, tiling in both axes.

image.prompt:
A SEAMLESSLY TILING TOP-DOWN GROUND TEXTURE. This is a flat material swatch, not a photograph of a scene or of an object. The camera looks straight down at the ground from directly overhead, perfectly orthographic, with no perspective, no horizon, no vanishing point and no tilt.

The surface: Flat square of red clay brick paving seen as a single unbroken surface, rectangular bricks laid flat in a herringbone pattern of interlocking diagonal pairs with fine sandy joints, colour varying brick to brick from orange to deep red-brown, edge to edge brick only, no kerb and no border Materials: Seamlessly tiling fired clay pavers ranging orange, terracotta and dark red-brown with a matte slightly gritty face, kiln blushes and dark scorch marks on scattered bricks, faces worn smooth and lightly polished along the walked lines, pale sand in the joints with moss and small weeds in the shaded runs, a chalky white efflorescence bloom in a few patches, chipped corners and one or two cracked bricks; the herringbone must wrap on all four edges so a run of tiles gives one continuous unbroken pattern.

Scale: the square shown covers exactly 8 by 8 metres of real ground, so every stone, block, slab, joint, marking, rut and tuft in it is drawn at its true size relative to that. Do not zoom in on a detail and do not pull back to show a wider scene.

Tiling: the texture must repeat seamlessly on all four edges. What runs off the left edge continues onto the right edge, and what runs off the top continues onto the bottom, exactly. No feature may be cut in half at an edge without its other half appearing at the opposite edge. Laid out four by four this must read as one continuous surface with no visible grid, no repeated landmark feature and no seam.

Framing: the surface fills the entire frame edge to edge and corner to corner. There is no border, no frame, no margin, no backdrop, no background, no matte and no empty space of any kind. The ground continues past every edge of the image.

Nothing stands on it and nothing bounds it: no kerb, no wall, no step, no gutter, no drain, no manhole cover, no grass verge, no plants, no people, no vehicles, no furniture, no objects, no litter, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows.

Lighting: flat, even, shadowless overhead illumination, like a lightbox. The image is the surface's true albedo. No sun, no cast shadows, no directional highlights, no specular blowout, no vignette, no gradient across the frame, no baked ambient occlusion in the corners and crevices, no light falloff towards the edges -- an uneven frame cannot tile, because its bright side would meet its dark side at every seam.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, realistic material, real surface wear and staining. Not stylised, not cartoon, not a 3D render preview, not a tiled collage of separate photographs, not a pattern illustration.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

name: Red Brick Herringbone Paving Tile
nameTh: พื้นอิฐแดงลายก้างปลา
notes: One flat quad, 8 x 8 m, lying in the ground plane at y=0 -- two triangles, one geometry, one draw call, one PBR material, and nothing else. The entire surface reads out of the texture; not a single brick is modelled, and the joint recesses and worn brick faces are carried by the normal and AO maps. This is a member of the kit's ground-surface tile set: every tile in that set is 8 x 8 m, sits at y=0, uses pivot base-center and snaps on the kit's 8 m grid, so it butts flush against any other ground tile and against the asphalt road tiles, and the raised Concrete Sidewalk Strip (2.0 m wide, 0.15 m tall) sits alongside as a separate object. Red clay brick paving in Thailand belongs to temple grounds, garden and park paths, resort and hotel forecourts and older municipal squares, so this is the warm counterpart to the grey interlocking concrete paver that covers everyday commercial ground. Herringbone is deliberately the pattern rather than a running bond, because a herringbone is invariant under a 90 degree rotation: that makes this tile fully FOUR-way rotationally symmetric, so it drops in at any of four orientations and a large paved area does not read as a grid of identical copies. The pattern pitch must divide 8 m evenly and wrap on all four edges, or every tile boundary shows a broken diagonal -- that is the first thing to check on the generated texture, and a herringbone is unforgiving about it because the eye follows the diagonals straight across a seam. Budget overridden explicitly to 2 triangles / 1 draw call / 1 material / 1 unique geometry instead of the hero2x its 8 m footprint would derive: footprint drives the class, but there is no geometry here to spend a class budget on. Quality comes entirely from a high-end tiling PBR texture set and not from mesh detail; that is the whole bet of this piece. No destruction groups: a ground tile is static level geometry, not a breakable.
